subsection: 1. Renewable and non-renewable resources in the economy

notes.h: Resources and how they are classed
notes.b: A resource is anything in the environment that people use to meet their needs. Resources are classed by whether nature can replace them.
points: Resources include energy, minerals, water, soil, forests, fish, land and scenery.
Non-renewable (stock, finite) resources formed over millions of years, so they are used up far faster than they form and will eventually run out: coal, oil, natural gas, peat, metal ores and uranium.
Renewable (flow) resources are replaced naturally and will not run out however much is used: wind, solar, hydro (running water), wave, tidal and geothermal heat.

Some resources are renewable only if managed sustainably: forests, fish stocks, soils, groundwater and biomass. Overuse turns them into exhausted resources, as happens with fish stocks (see the note Sustainable economic development).

notes.h: Fossil fuels, peat and nuclear energy
points: Fossil fuels (coal, oil, natural gas and peat) formed from the remains of plants or marine organisms buried and compressed over millions of years; burning them releases the carbon they stored.
Peat is non-renewable: a bog grows only about 1 mm a year, far slower than it is cut.
Nuclear energy from uranium is an alternative to fossil fuels with low carbon emissions, but it is not renewable because uranium is finite.

notes.h: Primary energy, electricity and the economy
points: Primary energy is energy in its raw form, such as oil, gas or wind. Electricity is a secondary form made from primary sources.
Energy powers industry, transport, farming and homes, so resources are central to the economy.
Energy security means a secure and affordable supply that is not disrupted by price shocks or supply cuts.
A country that imports its energy pays a large import bill and is exposed to price shocks and supply cuts.

notes.b: Ireland has few fossil fuels of its own, so it depends heavily on imported energy.
points: Import dependence (the share of energy bought from abroad): Ireland imported close to 90% of its energy in the years before Corrib gas came ashore in 2015.
The share fell after Corrib began and has risen again as Corrib's output declines. In the early 2020s Ireland still imported about three-quarters of its energy (SEAI).
Early 2020s primary energy mix (SEAI): oil just under half and the largest single source; natural gas about a third; renewables a little over a tenth; coal and peat small and falling.
All of Ireland's oil is imported.
Oil is used mainly for transport and home heating.
Whitegate, Co. Cork, is Ireland's only oil refinery.
Kinsale Head gas field, off Co. Cork, was discovered in 1971 and began production in 1978 as Ireland's first commercial gas field. Production ended in 2020 when the field was depleted.
Corrib gas field, off north-west Co. Mayo, was discovered in 1996 and first flowed in December 2015. Its gas is processed at Bellanaboy, Co. Mayo.
For a time after 2015 Corrib supplied over half of Ireland's gas. Its output is now declining.
Most of Ireland's gas now comes from Britain through interconnector pipelines from Moffat, Scotland.
Gas is the largest single source of Irish electricity.

Ireland's native coalfields are small and long closed: Arigna, Co. Roscommon, where mining ended in 1990 and which is now the Arigna Mining Experience (see the note A Peripheral Irish Region), and Castlecomer, Co. Kilkenny.
Moneypoint, Co. Clare, on the Shannon Estuary, is an ESB coal-fired station opened in 1985. At about 900 MW it is Ireland's largest power station.
Moneypoint burned imported coal, brought in by large ships to its deep-water jetty.
Moneypoint stopped burning coal in 2025.
Bord na Móna, the State peat company, was founded in 1946.
Peat-fired stations at Lanesborough (Lough Ree) and Shannonbridge (West Offaly) closed in December 2020. Bord na Móna ended all peat harvesting in January 2021.
Edenderry, Co. Offaly, switched from peat to biomass.
Bellacorick, Co. Mayo: the peat station closed in 2003 and was replaced by wind farms on the cutaway bog.
Cutaway bogs are reused. Lough Boora Discovery Park, Co. Offaly, has turned a cutaway bog into parkland, wetlands and walking and cycling trails.

Ardnacrusha, on the River Shannon near Limerick, was built by the German firm Siemens and opened in 1929 as the Shannon Scheme. The ESB was set up in 1927 to run it, and for some years it supplied most of the country's electricity.
Other stations: Poulaphouca on the River Liffey, Co. Wicklow; Inniscarra and Carrigadrohid on the River Lee, Co. Cork; and Cathaleen's Fall at Ballyshannon on the River Erne, Co. Donegal.
Turlough Hill, Co. Wicklow, opened in 1974 as an ESB pumped-storage station. Water is pumped uphill when demand is low and released through turbines at peak times.

notes.b: Wind is Ireland's main renewable source.
points: Wind supplied about a third of Irish electricity in the early 2020s. Renewables, mostly wind, supplied about two-fifths.
Strong, frequent Atlantic winds make the western coasts and uplands the best sites for wind farms.
Bellacorick wind farm, Co. Mayo (1992), was Ireland's first commercial wind farm. Oweninny wind farm was built on the same cutaway bog.
Galway Wind Park, Connemara, completed in 2017, is one of Ireland's largest onshore wind farms.
Arklow Bank Wind Park, off Co. Wicklow, opened in 2004 as Ireland's first offshore wind farm, with seven turbines.

notes.h: Solar, wave, tidal, geothermal and biomass in Ireland
points: Solar power has grown rapidly since the early 2020s, through large solar farms on farmland and panels on rooftops. SEAI grants support home installations.
The Atlantic Marine Energy Test Site off Belmullet, Co. Mayo, is Ireland's wave-energy test site.
Geothermal energy is limited to low-temperature ground-source heat pumps.
Tidal energy harnesses the rise and fall of the sea, and it is at an early stage in Ireland.
Biomass (wood and energy crops) and biofuels are the remaining renewable sources.
Ireland's 2020 EU target was 16% of gross final energy consumption from renewables.
Ireland reached only about 13.5% and missed the target. It was one of the furthest from its target of any EU member state.
Climate Action Plan: 80% of electricity from renewables by 2030, and at least 5 GW of offshore wind by 2030.
Climate Action and Low Carbon Development (Amendment) Act 2021: cut greenhouse gas emissions by 51% by 2030, compared with 2018, and reach climate neutrality (net zero) by 2050.

notes.h: Why Ireland lagged behind other EU countries on renewables
points: Heavy dependence on cars and road freight for transport.
Oil used for home heating in a dispersed rural settlement pattern.
Slow planning and grid connection for wind farms.
No large hydro potential left for new schemes.
A late start on offshore wind.
Strong economic and population growth raising energy demand.
The East-West Interconnector, opened in 2012, links Co. Dublin to north Wales by electricity cable.
The Celtic Interconnector, from Co. Cork to Brittany, France, is under construction and due to link Ireland to the EU mainland grid in the late 2020s.

notes.h: Energy use by sector in Ireland
points: Transport is the largest energy-using sector in Ireland (SEAI).
Heat for homes and businesses comes next, then electricity generation for industry and services.
Data centres used about a fifth of Ireland's metered electricity in 2023 (CSO). Most are in the Dublin region.

notes.b: Europe depends heavily on imported energy, and its main oil and gas comes from the North Sea and from suppliers outside the EU.
points: The EU imports close to three-fifths of its energy (early 2020s, Eurostat).
The North Sea, shared by the UK and Norway, is Europe's main oil and gas province.
Norway is not an EU member but is one of the EU's main gas suppliers, by pipeline.
Before 2022 Russia supplied about two-fifths of the EU's imported gas.
Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022. Gas and electricity prices soared across Europe.
REPowerEU plan, May 2022: cut dependence on Russian fossil fuels by saving energy, importing more liquefied natural gas (LNG, much of it from the USA) and speeding up renewables.
Russia's share of EU gas imports has since fallen sharply.
Nuclear power supplies about two-thirds of France's electricity.
The Energiewende (energy transition) is Germany's long-term switch to renewables.
After the Fukushima disaster in Japan in March 2011, Germany decided to phase out nuclear power. Its last three reactors closed on 15 April 2023.
Germany still burns lignite (brown coal) from huge open-cast mines in the Rhineland. A 2020 law sets 2038 at the latest as the end of coal-fired power.
Coal generates well over half of Poland's electricity (early 2020s).
Wind supplies about half of Denmark's electricity (2020s).
Denmark was an early leader in wind power and is home to the turbine maker Vestas.

notes.h: Norway and Iceland: hydro and geothermal (European, not EU members)
points: Hydroelectric power supplies about 90% of Norway's electricity, from its mountains, high rainfall and glacial lakes.
Geothermal and hydro supply almost all of Iceland's electricity, and about 9 in 10 Icelandic homes are heated geothermally.
The EU target of 20% renewable energy by 2020 was achieved, at about 22%.
The revised Renewable Energy Directive (2023) requires at least 42.5% renewable energy by 2030.
Renewables supplied about a quarter of EU gross final energy consumption in 2023.

notes.h: Patterns of energy consumption in the EU
points: Fossil fuels (oil, gas and coal) still supply most of the EU's energy. Oil is the largest single source, mainly for transport.
Transport, households and industry each take roughly a quarter to a third of final energy. Services take a smaller share.
Core industrial countries, such as Germany and France, consume most of the energy.
Resource-rich countries, such as Norway, export energy.
Peripheral countries, such as Ireland, depend on imports.

keyTerms.definition: Anything in the environment that people use to meet their needs, such as energy, minerals, water or soil.
A resource formed over millions of years and used up faster than it forms, so it will eventually run out.
A resource that is replaced naturally and will not run out however much is used.
A fuel, such as coal, oil, natural gas or peat, formed from buried plant or marine remains.
Energy in its raw form, such as oil, gas or wind, before it is converted into another form.
The share of a country's energy supply that it buys from abroad.
A secure and affordable supply of energy that is not easily disrupted by price shocks or supply cuts.
A cable or pipeline that links one country's energy network to another's.
A hydroelectric method that pumps water uphill when demand is low and releases it through turbines at peak times.
Renewable organic material, such as wood or energy crops, burned or converted to energy.

factCards.term: Peat and nuclear energy: why neither is renewable
factCards.definition: Peat: a bog grows only about 1 mm a year, far slower than it is cut, so it is used up faster than it forms. Nuclear: uranium is finite, so nuclear is a low-carbon alternative to fossil fuels but not renewable.

factCards.term: Ireland's energy import dependence: how it has changed
factCards.definition: Ireland imported close to 90% of its energy before Corrib gas came ashore in 2015; the share fell after Corrib began and has risen again as Corrib's output declines; in the early 2020s Ireland still imported about three-quarters (SEAI).

factCards.term: Ireland's primary energy mix in the early 2020s
factCards.definition: Oil just under half, the largest single source (all imported, used mainly for transport and home heating, refined at Whitegate, Co. Cork, the only refinery); natural gas about a third; renewables a little over a tenth; coal and peat small and falling (SEAI).

factCards.term: Kinsale Head and Corrib gas fields: key dates
factCards.definition: Kinsale Head, off Co. Cork: discovered 1971, produced from 1978 as Ireland's first commercial gas field, ended 2020 when depleted. Corrib, off north-west Co. Mayo: discovered 1996, first gas December 2015, processed at Bellanaboy.

factCards.term: Natural gas in Ireland: where it comes from now
factCards.definition: For a time after 2015 Corrib supplied over half of Ireland's gas, but its output is declining; most gas now comes from Britain through interconnector pipelines from Moffat, Scotland. Gas is the largest single source of Irish electricity.

factCards.term: Coal in Ireland: native coalfields and Moneypoint
factCards.definition: Arigna, Co. Roscommon (mining ended 1990) and Castlecomer, Co. Kilkenny are long closed. Moneypoint, Co. Clare, on the Shannon Estuary: ESB station opened 1985, Ireland's largest (about 900 MW), burned imported coal shipped to its deep-water jetty until 2025.

factCards.term: Peat power in Ireland: how it ended
factCards.definition: Bord na Móna, the State peat company, was founded in 1946. Peat stations at Lanesborough (Lough Ree) and Shannonbridge (West Offaly) closed in December 2020; all peat harvesting ended in January 2021; Edenderry, Co. Offaly, switched to biomass.

factCards.term: Cutaway bogs: two examples of reuse
factCards.definition: Bellacorick, Co. Mayo: the peat station closed in 2003 and was replaced by wind farms on the cutaway bog, including Oweninny. Lough Boora Discovery Park, Co. Offaly: parkland, wetlands and walking and cycling trails.

factCards.term: Hydroelectric power in Ireland: name the stations and their rivers
factCards.definition: Ardnacrusha on the Shannon near Limerick (Siemens, 1929; the ESB was set up in 1927 to run it); Poulaphouca on the Liffey; Inniscarra and Carrigadrohid on the Lee; Cathaleen's Fall on the Erne; Turlough Hill, Co. Wicklow (1974), pumped storage.

factCards.term: Wind energy in Ireland: its share and why it suits Ireland
factCards.definition: Wind, Ireland's main renewable, supplied about a third of electricity in the early 2020s and all renewables about two-fifths (but only a little over a tenth of primary energy). Strong, frequent Atlantic winds make western coasts and uplands the best sites.

factCards.term: Name three Irish wind farms, onshore and offshore
factCards.definition: Bellacorick, Co. Mayo (1992), Ireland's first commercial wind farm; Galway Wind Park, Connemara (completed 2017), one of the largest onshore; Arklow Bank Wind Park, off Co. Wicklow (2004), the first offshore, with seven turbines.

factCards.term: Solar, wave, geothermal and biomass in Ireland: one fact each
factCards.definition: Solar: rapid growth since the early 2020s (solar farms, rooftop panels, SEAI home grants); wave: Atlantic Marine Energy Test Site off Belmullet, Co. Mayo; geothermal: only low-temperature ground-source heat pumps; biomass: Edenderry power station, Co. Offaly, switched from peat to biomass.

factCards.term: Ireland's 2020 EU renewable energy target: was it met?
factCards.definition: No. The target was 16% of gross final energy consumption from renewables by 2020; Ireland reached only about 13.5%, one of the furthest from target of any EU member state.

factCards.term: Ireland's climate and energy targets for 2030 and 2050
factCards.definition: Climate Action Plan: 80% of electricity from renewables and at least 5 GW of offshore wind by 2030. Climate Action and Low Carbon Development (Amendment) Act 2021: cut emissions by 51% by 2030 (compared with 2018) and reach net zero by 2050.

factCards.term: Why Ireland lagged behind other EU countries on renewables
factCards.definition: Heavy reliance on cars and road freight; oil home heating in a dispersed rural settlement pattern; slow planning and grid connection for wind; no large hydro potential left; a late start on offshore wind; fast economic and population growth raising demand.

factCards.term: Ireland's electricity interconnectors: name two
factCards.definition: East-West Interconnector, Co. Dublin to north Wales, opened 2012; Celtic Interconnector, Co. Cork to Brittany, France, under construction and due in the late 2020s to link Ireland to the EU mainland grid.

factCards.term: Energy use by sector in Ireland: order and a fast-growing user
factCards.definition: Transport is the largest energy-using sector (SEAI), then heat for homes and businesses, then electricity generation for industry and services. Data centres used about a fifth of metered electricity in 2023 (CSO), most in the Dublin region.

factCards.term: European energy supply: imports and the main suppliers
factCards.definition: The EU imports close to three-fifths of its energy (early 2020s, Eurostat). The North Sea (UK and Norway) is the main oil and gas province; Norway, outside the EU, pipes gas to it. Core Germany and France consume most; peripheral Ireland imports.

factCards.term: Russia, Ukraine and REPowerEU: what happened in 2022
factCards.definition: Before 2022 Russia supplied about two-fifths of the EU's imported gas. Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022 and gas and electricity prices soared. REPowerEU (May 2022): save energy, import more LNG (much from the USA), speed up renewables.

factCards.term: France and Poland: contrasting electricity mixes
factCards.definition: France: nuclear power supplies about two-thirds of its electricity. Poland: coal generates well over half of its electricity (early 2020s).

factCards.term: Germany's Energiewende: three key facts
factCards.definition: A long-term switch to renewables. After Fukushima (March 2011) Germany phased out nuclear; its last three reactors closed on 15 April 2023. It still burns lignite from open-cast mines in the Rhineland; a 2020 law ends coal power by 2038 at the latest.

factCards.term: Denmark, Norway and Iceland: how each makes its electricity
factCards.definition: Denmark: wind about half, an early leader and home of turbine maker Vestas. Norway: hydro about 90% (mountains, high rainfall, glacial lakes). Iceland: geothermal and hydro almost all; about 9 in 10 homes heated geothermally.

factCards.term: EU renewable energy targets: 2020 and 2030
factCards.definition: The 20% target for 2020 was achieved, at about 22%; the revised Renewable Energy Directive (2023) requires at least 42.5% by 2030; renewables supplied about a quarter of EU gross final energy consumption in 2023.

factCards.term: EU energy consumption: by fuel and by sector
factCards.definition: Fossil fuels still supply most of the EU's energy, and oil is the largest single source, mainly for transport. Transport, households and industry each take roughly a quarter to a third of final energy; services take less.

questions.prompt: Examine the use of renewable and non-renewable energy resources in Ireland.
questions.model: A resource is anything people use to meet their needs. Non-renewable resources such as coal, oil, natural gas and peat formed over millions of years and will run out, whereas renewable resources such as wind, solar, hydro, wave, tidal and geothermal are replaced naturally. Ireland has few fossil fuels of its own and imported close to 90% of its energy before Corrib gas came ashore in 2015, and it still imported about three-quarters of its energy in the early 2020s. Oil is the largest single source of primary energy, used mainly for transport and home heating, and all of it is imported through Whitegate, Co. Cork, Ireland's only refinery. Natural gas is about a third of primary energy: Kinsale Head, off Co. Cork, was Ireland's first commercial gas field from 1978 until production ended in 2020, and Corrib, off Co. Mayo, supplied over half of Irish gas for a time after 2015 before its output began to decline; most gas now comes from Britain by pipeline from Moffat, Scotland, and gas is the largest source of electricity. Coal is small and falling: Moneypoint, Co. Clare, opened in 1985 and burned imported coal until it stopped in 2025. Peat is non-renewable and is being phased out: the ESB's peat-fired stations at Lanesborough and Shannonbridge, supplied by Bord na Móna, closed in December 2020, harvesting ended in January 2021, and Edenderry switched to biomass. Renewables supply a little over a tenth of primary energy but about two-fifths of electricity. Hydro's major scheme is Ardnacrusha on the Shannon, opened in 1929, and Turlough Hill is a pumped-storage station, though little potential is left for large new schemes. Wind is the main renewable, supplying about a third of electricity, with Bellacorick, Co. Mayo, as the first commercial wind farm in 1992 and Arklow Bank, off Co. Wicklow, as the first offshore farm in 2004. Solar is growing rapidly, while wave energy is at the Belmullet test site. Ireland missed its 2020 target of 16% renewables, reaching about 13.5%, and its Climate Action Plan aims for 80% renewable electricity by 2030. Interconnectors to Wales (2012) and France (due in the late 2020s) improve energy security.

questions.prompt: Describe and explain patterns of energy production and consumption in Europe.
questions.model: The EU imports close to three-fifths of its energy, so its production and consumption are shaped by dependence on suppliers. The North Sea, shared by the UK and Norway, is Europe's main oil and gas province, and Norway, which is not an EU member, is one of the EU's main gas suppliers by pipeline. Before 2022 Russia supplied about two-fifths of the EU's imported gas. After Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022, prices soared, and the REPowerEU plan of May 2022 aimed to cut Russian fossil fuel dependence by saving energy, importing more LNG and speeding up renewables; Russia's share of gas imports has since fallen sharply. Energy mixes vary by country. France gets about two-thirds of its electricity from nuclear power. Germany is pursuing the Energiewende, phasing out nuclear after Fukushima with its last reactors closing on 15 April 2023, but still burns lignite from open-cast mines in the Rhineland, with coal-fired power set to end by 2038 at the latest. Poland generates well over half of its electricity from coal. Denmark gets about half its electricity from wind, and Norway gets about 90% from hydro, using its mountains and high rainfall. Iceland relies almost entirely on geothermal and hydro. Fossil fuels still supply most of the EU's energy, with oil the largest single source, mainly for transport. Transport, households and industry each take roughly a quarter to a third of final energy. Core industrial countries such as Germany and France consume most, resource-rich Norway exports energy, and peripheral countries such as Ireland depend on imports. The EU target of 20% renewables by 2020 was achieved at about 22%, the revised Directive requires at least 42.5% by 2030, and renewables supplied about a quarter of gross final energy consumption in 2023.

questions.prompt: Explain two reasons why Ireland was far from its 2020 renewable energy target.
questions.model: First, Ireland's transport system relies heavily on cars and road freight, so transport demand is hard to switch to renewable energy. Second, slow planning and grid connection for wind farms delayed new projects, so Ireland reached only about 13.5% against a target of 16%.
